media_work.title: The Fear of Too Much Justice: Race, Poverty, and the Persistence of Inequality in the Criminal Courts
media_work.creator_name: Stephen B. Bright and James Kwak
media_work.format: Hardcover (368 pages); Paperback edition released April 2025
media_work.focus_or_theme: Examination of how the U.S. legal system fails to uphold constitutional rights of defendants, especially poor defendants and people of color
media_work.key_statistics: Not specifically mentioned in available sources

media_item.case_details_raw:
While specific case details are not provided in the available sources, the book examines how race, poverty, and inequality contribute to wrongful convictions and other injustices in the criminal courts. According to John Grisham's endorsement, Stephen Bright has spent forty years working "to protect the poor and innocent, and to expose the truth behind capital punishment, wrongful convictions, corrupt prosecutors, incompetent judges, and all the other bad actors who have ruined our system."

The book ranges from "people convicted of crimes and condemned to death because of their race and poverty to poor people squeezed for cash by private probation companies because of trivial violations." It also offers examples from places around the country that are making progress toward justice.
key_quotes_raw: "The book John Grisham calls 'a clear and poignant indictment of criminal injustice in America'"
"Everyone needs to read this book." —Poppy Harlow, CNN

"Only Steve Bright could write such a clear and poignant indictment of criminal injustice in America. For forty years he's waged hand-to-hand legal combat to protect the poor and innocent, and to expose the truth behind capital punishment, wrongful convictions, corrupt prosecutors, incompetent judges, and all the other bad actors who have ruined our system." —John Grisham

"An urgently needed analysis of our collective failure to confront and overcome racial bias and bigotry, the abuse of power, and the multiple ways in which the death penalty's profound unfairness requires its abolition." —Bryan Stevenson (in the foreword)
systemic_issues_raw: Racial bias and discrimination in the criminal justice system
Economic inequality and its impact on legal outcomes
Inadequate legal representation for poor defendants
Prosecutorial misconduct and abuse of power
The death penalty's disproportionate application to poor and minority defendants
Private probation companies exploiting poor defendants for profit
Failure to uphold constitutional rights, especially for marginalized communities
policy_recommendations_raw: The book offers "examples from places around the country that are making progress toward justice," suggesting it includes policy recommendations or best practices
Based on Bryan Stevenson's foreword, the book likely advocates for the abolition of the death penalty
Likely includes recommendations for addressing racial bias, economic inequality, and other systemic issues in the criminal justice system

Equal Justice Initiative (founded by Bryan Stevenson, who wrote the foreword)
Death Penalty Information Center (which featured the book)

research_notes_other.\"the_fear_of_too_much_justice:
Race, Poverty, and the Persistence of Inequality in the Criminal Courts" is a comprehensive examination of the failures of the U.S. criminal justice system, particularly as they affect poor defendants and people of color. The title references a quote from Supreme Court Justice Harry Blackmun, who in a death penalty case wrote about "a fear of too much justice" when the Court refused to address racial disparities in capital sentencing.
The book is co-authored by Stephen B. Bright, a renowned death penalty attorney who served as the director of the Southern Center for Human Rights and teaches law at Georgetown and Yale Universities, and James Kwak, a legal scholar who serves as vice chair of the Board of the Southern Center for Human Rights and has authored several books on economics and public policy.
According to available sources, the book offers a "heart-wrenching overview of how the criminal legal system fails to live up to the values of equality and justice." It examines various aspects of the criminal justice system, from wrongful convictions and death penalty cases to the exploitation of poor defendants by private probation companies.
The book includes a foreword by Bryan Stevenson, founder of the Equal Justice Initiative and author of "Just Mercy," who describes it as "an urgently needed analysis of our collective failure to confront and overcome racial bias and bigotry, the abuse of power, and the multiple ways in which the death penalty's profound unfairness requires its abolition."
While the available sources do not detail specific wrongful conviction cases featured in the book, John Grisham's endorsement suggests that Bright's forty years of experience working "to protect the poor and innocent, and to expose the truth behind capital punishment, wrongful convictions, corrupt prosecutors, incompetent judges, and all the other bad actors" informs the book's content.
The book not only identifies problems but also highlights solutions, offering "examples from places around the country that are making progress toward justice." This suggests a forward-looking approach that goes beyond critique to offer potential paths for reform.
Publishers Weekly described the book as an "urgent call to action" and "an invaluable resource," indicating its potential impact on criminal justice reform efforts. The book's release in paperback format in April 2025 suggests ongoing relevance and demand for its insights.
